title: Emmaus, slowly (Luke 24:13–35)
hook: stay with us, because it is towards evening

segments.voice: Yesterday, idle tales: the women's news from the empty tomb, and apostles who didn't believe it. Your line was not idle tales.

The same Sunday, in the afternoon. Two disciples are walking away from Jerusalem toward a village called Emmaus, about sixty furlongs off, seven miles or so. One is named Cleophas; the other Luke never names. They're going over everything that has happened, the way people do after a funeral. A stranger falls into step and asks what they're discussing. They stop, faces sad. Are you the only visitor in Jerusalem who doesn't know? Luke tells this slowly, and the slowness is the point.
screen: `TWO WALKING AWAY.` → `A STRANGER FALLS INTO STEP.` → `ARE YOU THE ONLY ONE WHO DOESN'T KNOW?`

segments.voice: They tell him the whole story, and their grief is in the past tense: we hoped that it was he that should have redeemed Israel. We hoped. The stranger walks them through the scriptures, beginning with Moses and all the prophets, showing what they said about the Christ. It takes miles. At the village, he makes as if to keep going, and they won't let him: "But they constrained him; saying: Stay with us, because it is towards evening, and the day is now far spent. And he went in with them." At table he takes bread, blesses it, breaks it, and gives it to them. "And their eyes were opened, and they knew him: and he vanished out of their sight." Their hearts, they say, were burning while he opened the scriptures on the road, and that same hour they go back to Jerusalem to tell how he was known to them in the breaking of bread. Catholic teaching sees the shape of the Mass here. First the word: the scriptures opened and explained. Then the table: bread taken, blessed, broken, given. Saint John Paul the Second built his letter for the Year of the Eucharist around this scene and titled it with the disciples' plea in Latin, Mane nobiscum Domine, stay with us, Lord. And notice: he doesn't force his way in. He would have walked on. The invitation is theirs. Luke shows the risen Christ waiting to be asked.
screen: `WE HOPED.` · `THE SCRIPTURES OPENED ON THE ROAD.` · `STAY WITH US, IT IS TOWARDS EVENING.` · `KNOWN IN THE BREAKING OF BREAD.`

segments.voice: Think back over today as if it were a road: where were you walking, what were you talking about, what did you hope for that didn't happen? Let it be there, the way it was for those two, and picture the evening coming in. If you pray, use their words, stay with us, because it is towards evening; if you don't, just notice what you'd want to stay with you tonight.
Emmaus. The village seven miles from Jerusalem where two disciples knew the risen Jesus in the breaking of bread. Nobody is certain where it was. Today's word.
Your line: stay with us. A plea at dusk, and a guest who said yes. Day four hundred eighty-eight, done.

howItsDone: Catholics hear the Emmaus story in Easter week and on the Third Sunday of Easter in one year of the cycle, and Catholic teaching points to it as the pattern of the Mass: the Liturgy of the Word, then the Liturgy of the Eucharist.

original.note: Latin, from the Vulgate of Luke 24:29: stay with us. John Paul II's 2004 letter takes its title from it.

trapdoor: what you thought: a story about two people who didn't recognize a friend.
what it means: the risen Christ is known when the scriptures are opened and the bread is broken, and he waits to be invited.
what a scholar hears: the four table verbs (took, blessed, broke, gave) echo the Last Supper; Emmaus's location is still debated.

chat.says: On the road to Emmaus, when did the two finally recognize Jesus?
options: At the table, when he took bread, blessed it, broke it and gave it to them.
Right away, as soon as he started walking beside them on the road.
Only later, when the other apostles in Jerusalem told them who it was.
chat.meaning: Luke says their eyes were opened at table, in the breaking of bread. The Church sees the Mass in it: the word, then the table.

Emmaus.meaning: a village about seven miles from Jerusalem

Cleophas.meaning: one of the two disciples walking to Emmaus

furlongs.meaning: an old distance; sixty is about seven miles

sources.ref: John Paul II, Mane nobiscum Domine (2004)

notes: Sixty furlongs (Douay; stadia) as about seven miles: standard; some manuscripts read 160 stadia. Confirm.
Emmaus's location is uncertain (Emmaus Nicopolis, el-Qubeibeh, Abu Ghosh, Motza and others proposed). Stated as uncertain.
'We had hoped' and the burning hearts (24:21, 24:32) are paraphrased without quotation marks. Confirm.
Lectionary: Emmaus is the Gospel for Wednesday of the Easter Octave and the Third Sunday of Easter, Year A. Confirm the howItsDone phrasing.
Original is Latin (Vulgate), not Greek, because the Catholic devotion and the papal letter use it; confirm this choice.
